title: JEZEBEL PAINTED HER EYES WHILE JUDGMENT WAS RIDING TOWARD HER
paragraphs: JEZEBEL PAINTED HER EYES WHILE JUDGMENT WAS RIDING TOWARD HER

She heard Jehu was coming. She knew what had happened. And instead of running, pleading, or repenting… she went to the mirror. But the most frightening part of this story may not be what Jezebel did. It may be how easily we do our own version of it.
There is something haunting about 2 Kings 9:30.
Not merely because someone is about to die.
Not merely because judgment has finally reached the palace.
But because of what Jezebel does when she hears that Jehu has arrived in Jezreel.
The Hebrew text says:
“וַיָּבֹא יֵהוּא יִזְרְעֶאלָה וְאִיזֶבֶל שָׁמְעָה וַתָּשֶׂם בַּפּוּךְ עֵינֶיהָ וַתֵּיטֶב אֶת־רֹאשָׁהּ וַתַּשְׁקֵף בְּעַד הַחַלּוֹן”
Vayyavo Yehu Yizre'elah… vattasem bappukh eineha, vatteitev et-roshah…
“And when Jehu was come to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it; and she painted her face, and tired her head, and looked out at a window.”
—2 Kings 9:30, KJV
The Hebrew is especially vivid.
וַתָּשֶׂם בַּפּוּךְ עֵינֶיהָ — vattasem bappukh eineha.
Literally, she put her eyes in or with pukh—eye paint, commonly understood as a dark cosmetic used around the eyes.
Then:
וַתֵּיטֶב אֶת־רֹאשָׁהּ — vatteitev et-roshah.
She adorned, beautified, or made her head presentable.
Jezebel heard that Jehu had come.
She painted her eyes.
She arranged herself.
And she went to the window.
Read that again.
Because the tragedy is deeper than makeup.
And before we go any further, we need to be careful with Scripture.
The Bible does not say that makeup itself was Jezebel's sin.
It does not say that a woman wearing cosmetics is behaving like Jezebel.

And although interpreters have proposed different motives for why Jezebel prepared her appearance—defiance, royal dignity, intimidation, seduction, or simply presenting herself as a queen before her enemy—the text itself does not explicitly tell us her motive.
So we should not pretend God said something He did not say.
What Scripture does tell us is far more sobering.
Jezebel had spent years resisting the God of Israel.
This was the woman connected with the promotion of Baal worship under Ahab.
The woman whose name stands behind the horrifying story of Naboth's vineyard.
Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard.
Naboth refused because the land was his ancestral inheritance.
Ahab went home miserable.
Then Jezebel intervened.
Letters were written in Ahab's name.
False witnesses were arranged.
Naboth was accused.
An innocent man was killed.
And when Naboth was dead, Ahab went down to possess the vineyard.
But God had seen everything.
That is the part human beings keep forgetting.
God sees what happens after the doors close.
God sees the conversation nobody recorded.
God sees the manipulation beneath respectable language.
God sees the secret browser history.
God sees the affair hidden behind deleted messages.
God sees the money nobody knows you took.
God sees the bitterness behind the smile.
God sees the ministry persona and the private addiction.
God sees what your spouse doesn't see.
God sees what your pastor doesn't see.
God sees what your followers don't see.
God sees what you have almost managed to convince yourself never happened.
And God saw Naboth.
Through Elijah, the Lord pronounced judgment upon Ahab's house and against Jezebel.
Years passed.
Imagine how easy it would have been to believe nothing was coming.
Morning after morning.
Meal after meal.
Season after season.
The palace still stood.
The servants still answered.
The queen was still the queen.
And that is one of sin's most dangerous illusions:
Because judgment has not happened yet, we begin imagining that God has forgotten.
But God's patience must never be confused with God's blindness.
And then one day…
hoofbeats.
Jehu was coming.
The man whom God had appointed through prophetic anointing to strike the house of Ahab was riding toward Jezreel.
Earlier in the chapter, the watchman sees his company approaching.
A messenger rides out.
Then another.
Neither returns.
Finally someone recognizes the furious driving.
“It is the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi; for he driveth furiously.”
The distance is closing.
Dust rises.
Horses move.
The palace receives the news.
And Jezebel hears.
This is where the story becomes almost unbearably human.
Because there is a moment when the truth finally reaches us.
The diagnosis comes.
The marriage breaks.
The secret gets discovered.
The child confronts you.
The addiction finally costs something.
The lie collapses.
The consequences arrive.
The sermon somehow feels as though the preacher has been reading your private life.
You sit alone after everyone has gone to sleep and suddenly the Holy Spirit puts His finger on the one thing you have spent years refusing to surrender.
And you know.
You know.
Something has to change.
Jezebel heard Jehu was coming.
And she painted her eyes.
Please don't reduce this to cosmetics.
The mirror is bigger than that.
Because some of us have learned to paint things too.
We paint pain with humor.
We paint loneliness with busyness.
We paint lust with secrecy.
We paint bitterness with religious vocabulary.
We paint pride with “discernment.”
We paint greed with “God's blessing.”
We paint an unhealthy marriage with smiling family photographs.
We paint spiritual emptiness with Christian posts.
We paint prayerlessness with ministry activity.
We paint rebellion with excuses.
We paint wounds with filters.
We paint exhaustion with “I'm blessed.”
We arrange our appearance while something inside us is collapsing.
And sometimes the most dangerous place you can be spiritually is not openly running from God.
It is learning how to look fine while running from God.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you still sing.
Maybe you still attend church.
Maybe your Bible still sits beside your bed.
Maybe you know exactly when to say “Amen.”
Maybe people ask you for prayer.
Maybe people think you're strong.
But you know what happens when the room becomes quiet.
You know what keeps calling you back.
You know the compromise.
You know the resentment.
You know the secret.
You know the name.
You know the face.
You know the website.
You know the bottle.
You know the conversation.
You know what you keep promising God you will stop “soon.”
And perhaps this article did not reach you so you could think about Jezebel.
Perhaps it reached you so you would stop hiding behind her.
Because the Bible was never given merely so we could identify villains.
It was given so the Word of God could expose us.
Hebrews says the Word is “quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword.”
It reaches beneath appearances.
Beneath explanations.
Beneath religious performance.
Down into the places where nobody else is allowed.
And here is where Jezebel's story becomes terrifying.
Jehu reaches the city.
She looks from the window.
She speaks.
But there is no recorded repentance.
No confession.
No cry for mercy.
No turning back to the God she had opposed.
Soon Jehu looks toward the window and calls:
“Who is on my side? who?”
Two or three eunuchs look down.
“Throw her down.”
And they do.
It is a brutal scene.
It should disturb us.
Biblical judgment is not entertainment.
Jezebel's death is not material for Christian mockery.
It is a warning about the seriousness of evil and the certainty that human power cannot ultimately place someone beyond God's judgment.
But now comes the question that changes this entire story.
What if you are reading this and realizing there is Jezebel-like defiance in your own heart?
What if you have resisted God?
What if you've manipulated people?
What if you've destroyed something precious?
What if you've been sexually immoral?
What if you've worshiped something other than God?
What if you've lied?
What if you've betrayed someone?
What if you've wasted years?
What if judgment would be deserved?
Is there hope for you?
Yes.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Scripture does not divide humanity into “people as bad as Jezebel” and “good people like us.”
“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
The respectable sinner.
The scandalous sinner.
The church sinner.
The street sinner.
The secret sinner.
The public sinner.
You.
Me.
Our hope has never been that our sins are prettier than someone else's.
Our hope is Christ.
And there was another day when judgment was approaching.
Except this time, the innocent One did not escape it.
Jesus Christ was nailed to a Roman cross.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Bleeding.
Rejected.
The sinless Son of God stood where sinners deserved to stand.
Isaiah had written centuries earlier:
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.”
And the New Testament announces the astonishing meaning of the cross:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
That is the Gospel.
Not paint over your sin.
Not rearrange your religious appearance.
Not become more impressive.
Not make people believe you're okay.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop decorating what Jesus died to deliver you from.
Stop defending what Christ is calling you to surrender.
Stop confusing God's patience with permission.
Stop staring through the window pretending you are untouchable.
The King is calling sinners home.
And here is the difference between condemnation without hope and Gospel conviction:
Conviction points toward a Savior.
Jesus did not come because we were already clean.
He came because we weren't.
He touched lepers.
He received sinners.
He ate with people respectable religion despised.
He forgave.
He restored.
He transformed.
He told the guilty to leave their lives of sin.
Grace never means sin does not matter.
Grace means sin mattered so much that the Son of God bore its cost to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
The cross does not tell you, “Your sin isn't serious.”
The cross tells you exactly how serious it is.
And then the cross tells you exactly how deep God's mercy goes.
Maybe that is why you're still reading.
Maybe somewhere between Jezebel's window and Christ's cross, your defenses started falling.
You are tired.
Tired of maintaining the image.
Tired of promising tomorrow.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of pretending prayerlessness isn't affecting you.
Tired of going back to the same sin.
Tired of looking spiritually alive while feeling spiritually numb.
Then don't paint over it again.
Bring it into the light.
You don't need another mask.
You need mercy.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice that.
Not some unrighteousness.
“All unrighteousness.”
That does not make confession a magical formula or repentance a performance that earns salvation.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ.
Biblical repentance is turning toward God—coming out of hiding, abandoning our claim to self-rule, and trusting the One who died and rose again.
You may have wrecked things you cannot repair by yourself.
There may still be consequences.
People you hurt may need time.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Restitution may be necessary.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every earthly consequence.
But your past does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left with which to repair his reputation.
Yet grace reached sinners.
This is why our message is not:
From scandal to respectability.
It is not:
From scandal to pretending it never happened.
It is not:
From scandal to better public relations.
It is:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting history as though the sin never happened.
He rewrites the sinner.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He gives a new heart.
He restores what can be restored.
He teaches us to walk differently.
He takes stories Satan would use only for shame and turns redeemed lives into testimonies of mercy.
Talk to God.
Now.
Not when you become worthy.
You won't.
Come because Christ is worthy.
Come because mercy is being offered.
Come because the Gospel is true.
And if you need words because your heart feels too heavy to manufacture them, simply say:

“Jesus, have mercy on me. I have sinned. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me. Change me. Teach me to follow You. I surrender what I've been hiding. I want You more than I want my sin.”
The prayer itself does not save you.
Jesus does.
Turn to Him.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, you don't have to tell strangers every private detail. But don't let shame push you back into darkness.
Or, if you're exhausted from fighting but refuse to abandon your faith:
“I'm still fighting.”
If you need believers to stand with you in prayer:
“Pray for me.”
Someone reading beneath your comment may desperately need to know they are not the only person fighting.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because Jezebel's makeup is the point.
And when that day comes, remember the window.
Remember the hoofbeats.
Remember the cross.
Then remember the empty tomb.
Send it privately to the person you know is hurting.
The lukewarm Christian.
The exhausted parent.
The secret struggler.
The person who thinks they've sinned too much.
Even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is about pretending to be good.
Let them discover that Christianity is ultimately about Christ saving sinners.
God cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be earned.
But Christian ministry does require people willing to help carry truth farther.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
It doesn't.
Share because someone may need the message.
And never forget what happened at that window.
Jezebel heard judgment approaching and prepared her appearance.
But you are reading this while mercy is still calling.
So don't merely fix what people can see.
Don't paint the eyes while the soul is starving.
Don't arrange the outside while rebellion is destroying the inside.
Don't spend another night protecting the very thing Jesus died to free you from.
Come out of hiding.
Come to the cross.
Come to Christ.
Because the most tragic thing about Jezebel's final appearance was never the paint around her eyes.
It was that Scripture records no repentance in her heart.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing about your story could be that yours does not have to end the same way.
The window does not have to be your ending.
The cross can become your turning point.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus Christ is alive.
Grace is still calling sinners home.
And as long as Christ is rewriting lives, your worst chapter does not have to become your final one.
You can keep painting over the ruins—or you can finally hand Jesus the story you have been trying to hide.
